studies.title: When populism rises, green packaging quietly disappears
studies.paper_title: Populism and sustainable marketing practices: Insights from consumer-packaged goods manufacturers’ new product launches
studies.journal: Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science
studies.the_study: Researchers treated the 2017 US announcement that it would exit the Paris Agreement as a quasi-natural experiment and ran a difference-in-differences analysis on a global sample of new product launches by consumer-packaged goods manufacturers. Firms more exposed to anti-climate-action populism measurably cut back on environmentally friendly packaging in subsequent launches. The pullback was weaker where subnational institutions pushed the other way — greater economic freedom and tighter local cultures blunted the retreat.
studies.why_it_matters: It shows sustainability commitments in packaging are far more politically contingent than corporate messaging implies, flexing with the perceived direction of government signals rather than with consumer demand alone.
studies.story_angle_primary: If your sustainable packaging roadmap is justified internally by regulatory expectation rather than consumer or retailer pull, it is vulnerable the moment the political wind shifts — a good prompt to audit which green commitments would survive a hostile policy environment, and how a visible retreat would read to stakeholders who were told the commitment was values-driven.
studies.story_angle_secondary: The eco-friendly packaging on a shelf is partly a political artifact: the same brand may make greener choices in one market or one election cycle than another, which is worth remembering when a company presents its packaging as a matter of principle.
studies.caveats: Observational quasi-experiment rather than a randomized design; centers on one policy shock in one country and on packaging choices in new launches, which is a narrow slice of sustainability behavior; no consumer response measured.
studies.verdict_notes: Design (quasi-natural experiment, difference-in-differences, global CPG launch sample), direction of effect, and both moderators (economic freedom, cultural tightness) are reported faithfully; caveats correctly note the observational design and absence of consumer outcomes.

studies.title: Big Pharma's pandemic tweets: dry facts beat upbeat framing
studies.paper_title: Dealing with misinformation in times of crises: an analysis of pharmaceutical companies’ corporate social media communication
studies.the_study: Researchers analyzed 6,466 tweets posted by six major pharmaceutical companies during 2020–2021, combining BERT-based topic modeling, lexicon-based detection of misinformation-countering strategies, and emotion analysis, then linked content features to likes and retweets. Science-based content drew significantly more engagement than other content types; "boosting" accurate information was far more common than directly refuting falsehoods and was also more widely amplified; and neutral, factual framing outperformed positively framed messaging.
studies.why_it_matters: In a contested information environment, perceived epistemic credibility — not emotional warmth or optimism — appears to drive audience amplification of corporate messages.
studies.story_angle_primary: Communications teams facing a misinformation flashpoint can test the counterintuitive option: lead with plain, neutral evidence and amplify what is true rather than publicly rebutting what is false. This is correlational engagement data from one industry and one platform, so it is a hypothesis to test in your own channels, not a proven rulebook.
studies.story_angle_secondary: It suggests audiences in a crisis reward sober information over cheerleading — and that the loudest corrective replies are not necessarily the ones that travel.
studies.caveats: Single platform (Twitter/X), single industry, six firms, and one extraordinary crisis period; engagement metrics are a weak proxy for belief change or behavior; associations are correlational and content categories rest on lexicon-based coding.
studies.verdict_notes: Sample (6,466 tweets, six firms, 2020-2021), methods, and all three findings match the abstract; correlational nature and single-platform/single-industry limits are flagged.

studies.title: Why companies cannot count the emissions hiding in their supply base
studies.paper_title: Carbon accounting in the supply chain: investigating its antecedents and consequences for organizations
studies.the_study: Using data on 1,142 firms, researchers built a new empirical method for estimating emissions embedded in a company's supply base — the Scope 3 territory beyond its own operations and purchased energy. Greater geographical and industrial diversity in the supplier network significantly increased supply base emissions, with buyer network influence and supplier interconnectedness moderating those effects.
studies.why_it_matters: Most of a consumer brand's carbon footprint sits with its suppliers, and this quantifies a structural driver — supply chain sprawl — that firms rarely acknowledge when making public climate claims.
studies.story_angle_primary: Before signing off on another net-zero communication, check whether your sourcing strategy is working against your climate targets: diversifying suppliers across more countries and industries, usually framed as resilience, may be inflating the emissions you will eventually have to report and defend.
studies.story_angle_secondary: When a brand advertises its carbon numbers, the figures typically cover its own factories and electricity — the far bigger share buried in its suppliers is often not measured at all.
studies.caveats: Observational cross-sectional firm data, so causal claims are limited; relies on voluntary and incomplete emissions disclosure, which the authors themselves flag as a data constraint; no consumer or reputational outcomes tested.
studies.verdict_notes: Sample (1,142 firms), drivers and moderators are reported correctly; the "Why it matters" and consumer angle upgrade the abstract's "substantial portion" of emissions to "most"/"far bigger share."

studies.title: Consumers say they'd rather be regulated than lectured on plastic
studies.paper_title: Coordinating Individual and System Change in the Marketing System: The TISI Framework for a Circular Plastics Economy
studies.the_study: Researchers studying single-use plastic milk packaging in New Zealand combined 20 consumer interviews with a best-worst scaling survey of 400 consumers to map what actually stops people from reducing plastic. Most of the barriers people named were "opportunity" constraints built into the retail and packaging system — no refill option, no return infrastructure — rather than gaps in knowledge or motivation. When ranking policy options, respondents preferred incentives and regulation over information-only campaigns. The authors package this into a framework (TISI) that separates consumers' market role (purchase, use, return, refill) from their citizen role (acceptance, perceived fairness, willingness to comply).
studies.why_it_matters: It suggests the standard sustainability playbook — awareness campaigns and on-pack nudges — is aimed at the wrong constraint, and that consumers may be more willing to accept rules and incentives than brands assume.
studies.story_angle_primary: Brands running recycling or refill campaigns could test whether the bottleneck is really consumer awareness or missing infrastructure before spending on another education push; the data here also hints that publicly backing regulation may be less reputationally risky with consumers than companies fear, though that was measured in one category in one country.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For shoppers, this is validation of a common frustration: people often want to cut plastic but have no practical way to return or refill, and the research suggests the burden has been misplaced on individual virtue.
studies.caveats: Single country (New Zealand) and a single category (milk packaging); stated preferences and rankings rather than observed purchase or return behavior; modest survey sample (N=400) alongside 20 interviews.
studies.verdict_notes: Mixed-method design (20 interviews plus best-worst scaling survey of 400), New Zealand milk packaging context, barrier findings and policy preferences all match; the digest correctly frames these as stated preferences. The citizen-role list omits "collective support," a trivial truncation.

studies.title: Green business models scale just as well as the ordinary kind — but only via the same boring levers
studies.paper_title: Do sustainable business models scale differently than business model configurations with lower environmental ambitions? A comparative analysis of business model scaling performance among sharing-mobility providers
studies.the_study: Researchers applied fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis to 21 sharing-mobility providers, modeling market scaling as a function of five design choices: environmental ambitions, alignment with public stakeholders, breadth of value propositions, digital intensity, and revenue-stream diversification. Six configurations emerged, four tied to successful scaling and two to failure. Firms with strong environmental ambitions and close public-sector alignment scaled about as well as those without; what consistently separated winners from losers in both groups was having multiple value propositions or diversified revenue streams. Successfully scaled firms also showed congruence between their green ambitions and their public-stakeholder alignment.
studies.why_it_matters: It pushes back on the assumption that sustainability commitments are a drag on growth, while deflating the idea that they are themselves a growth engine — the commercial fundamentals still do the work.
studies.story_angle_primary: For leaders weighing how hard to lean into environmental positioning: this evidence suggests genuine green ambition need not cost scalability, but it also won't substitute for portfolio breadth and revenue diversification — and half-committing (green claims without matching public-sector alignment) sits in the failure configurations.
studies.story_angle_secondary: A useful lens for consumers evaluating shared-mobility services: the ones that survive tend to be those selling several things to several customer types, not necessarily the greenest or the most digital.
studies.caveats: Very small sample of firms (21) in one sector (sharing mobility); configurational analysis identifies patterns of co-occurrence, not causation; no consumer-level data.
studies.verdict_notes: fsQCA on 21 providers, five design choices, six configurations (four success, two failure) and the three implications are accurately conveyed; one marketer angle states a claim about the failure configurations that the abstract does not make.

studies.title: PR agencies are quietly using AI — but in Arabic, humans are still doing the hard part
studies.paper_title: Sociolinguistic compatibility in AI adoption: extending DoI–TOE in public relations
studies.the_study: Through 20 semi-structured interviews with senior PR practitioners, association leaders and academics across six Arab countries, plus a directed content analysis of global and regional industry guidelines, researchers mapped where AI is actually being used in public relations. Adoption is early-stage and narrow, concentrated in content assistance, media intelligence and reputation monitoring, driven by efficiency pressure and client expectations. The main brakes are skills gaps, thin Arabic-language tooling and unclear governance. Global industry discourse converges on "augmentation" with disclosure and human oversight, but the authors argue that in under-resourced languages, maintaining cultural and linguistic fit is itself substantial hidden human labor.
studies.why_it_matters: Reputation work depends on tone and cultural nuance, and this suggests the efficiency case for AI in communications weakens sharply outside English — a gap that global agencies and in-house teams rarely budget for.
studies.story_angle_primary: Communications leaders running multilingual teams could audit where AI output actually requires rewriting rather than editing, treat localization as a staffed production stage rather than a tool setting, and consider making sociolinguistic review an explicit step in human-in-the-loop policies.
studies.story_angle_secondary: It explains why brand messaging in some languages can read as oddly flat or off-key: the tools behind it were built for English, and the cultural correction is done by people whose work is largely invisible.
studies.caveats: Qualitative interview study with a small, purposively selected senior sample (N=20) in one region; cross-regional comparison rests on documents rather than primary data; practitioner perceptions, not measured AI performance or audience response.
studies.verdict_notes: Method (20 interviews across six countries plus directed content analysis), adoption areas, drivers, barriers and the sociolinguistic-labour argument all match; the "Why it matters" generalizes beyond Arabic to all non-English contexts.

studies.title: What makes communicators feel like crisis leaders: ethics support and equity resources
studies.paper_title: Crisis Leadership in Public Relations: Examining the Roles of Ethics Resources, Equity Support, and Crisis Communication Effectiveness in the Pandemic Crisis
studies.the_study: An online survey of 1,044 public relations practitioners — nearly 43% with more than a decade of experience — examined how pandemic-era work challenges related to their sense of crisis leadership. Perceived access to ethics resources and organizational equity support both mediated the link between work strain and crisis leadership perceptions, and perceived effectiveness of the organization's crisis communication further shaped those indirect effects.
studies.why_it_matters: It points to concrete organizational investments — ethics guidance and equity support infrastructure — as levers that may strengthen how communications teams perform and see themselves under pressure, rather than treating crisis leadership as an individual trait.
studies.story_angle_primary: Comms leaders could treat ethics counsel and equity support as crisis-readiness infrastructure, not HR nice-to-haves, and test whether teams with documented ethics resources report stronger confidence and better-rated crisis output than those without.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Limited direct relevance for consumers, beyond the reminder that how well a company talks to the public in a crisis partly reflects how well it supports the people writing the statements.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional self-report survey — cannot establish causation; all variables are practitioner perceptions, including the outcome; retrospective pandemic framing; sample recruitment and country coverage not specified in the abstract.
studies.verdict_notes: N=1,044, the 42.7% experience figure, and the mediation structure (ethics resources and equity support mediating work challenge; crisis communication effectiveness intervening in the indirect effects) are all reported correctly; the "Why it matters" slips from perceptions to performance.

studies.title: Talking up AI wins positive sentiment but loses audience — unless you tie it to social good
studies.paper_title: Corporate AI communication: Public responses, organizational practice, and governance in Korea
studies.the_study: A mixed-method study of corporate AI communication in Korea combined a computational analysis of companies' social media posts (Study 1) with in-depth interviews with communication practitioners (Study 2). Corporate AI messaging was overwhelmingly instrumental — AI as business value, operational enabler or brand positioning — with little attention to societal or ethical implications. Although AI posts drew generally positive sentiment, they attracted less engagement and fewer positive comments than non-AI posts; framing AI within a corporate social responsibility context erased much of that engagement penalty, and AI messaging landed better at conventional firms than at high-tech firms where AI is simply expected.
studies.why_it_matters: Companies are racing to announce AI capabilities, but this evidence suggests the default "look how efficient we are" frame is the least engaging option and that the payoff depends heavily on whether audiences already expect AI from your category.
studies.story_angle_primary: Communications leaders could audit their own AI announcements for the instrumental-versus-societal balance and A/B test CSR-anchored framing against efficiency framing; the Korean pattern also hints that AI claims are a differentiator for legacy brands and a non-event for tech brands — worth checking in your own channel data before assuming it transfers.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For readers, the study is a window into how little of corporate AI talk addresses the questions the public actually asks — jobs, ethics, accountability — and how practitioners themselves admit they stay cautious about those topics even when aware of them.
studies.caveats: Single country (Korea) with a distinctive state-guided tech sector; social media engagement metrics are correlational, not causal; interview sample size not reported in the abstract; findings may not generalize to Western markets or to regulated industries.
studies.verdict_notes: Mixed-method Korean design, instrumental framing finding, engagement penalty, CSR moderation and the conventional-vs-high-tech contrast are all present; one verb overstates the size of the CSR effect.

studies.title: PR practitioners say using AI is no longer a choice — it is the price of staying competitive
studies.paper_title: Public relations AI practices: Neoliberalism, field theory, and professional dispositions within an AI-mediated habitus
studies.the_study: Interviews with 22 public relations practitioners explored how they are deploying AI bots and agentic systems for campaign development, decision-making and stakeholder research. Practitioners consistently described AI as compulsory for remaining competitive, as a form of self-optimization, and as a productivity multiplier — narratives the author reads as market logic shaping choices that practitioners experience as autonomous. At the same time, respondents leaned hard on professional judgment, context and a sense of responsibility, pointing to human oversight, risk management and formal governance as what keeps the work defensible in the absence of regulation.
studies.why_it_matters: It documents how AI adoption in reputation work is being driven less by evidence of better outcomes than by competitive anxiety — a dynamic that leaves governance to individual practitioners' discretion.
studies.story_angle_primary: Agency and in-house communications leaders can use this as a prompt to formalize what is currently informal: written AI governance, defined human sign-off points, and a candid internal conversation about whether AI use is being justified by results or by fear of falling behind.
studies.story_angle_secondary: The press releases, statements and stakeholder research shaping brand messages are increasingly AI-assisted, with oversight resting on individual professionals' judgment rather than any rulebook.
studies.caveats: Small qualitative interview sample (N=22); self-reported practice rather than observed outputs or performance data; heavily theory-driven interpretation (Foucault, Bourdieu) that readers may weigh differently; no measurement of whether AI use actually improved campaign results.
studies.verdict_notes: N=22 interviews, the compulsory/self-optimization/productivity narratives, the role of field dispositions and the absence of regulatory frameworks all match the abstract; caveats appropriately note the theory-driven reading and lack of outcome data. Singular "the author" is unverifiable from the abstract alone but harmless.

studies.title: In CSR posts, inviting people in beats who's doing the talking
studies.paper_title: CSR communication on social media: the impact of message source and co-creation cues on credibility, engagement, and e-WOM
studies.the_study: Researchers ran a 2x2 between-subjects experiment with 406 active Facebook users in India, varying who posted a corporate social responsibility message (a company vs. an NGO) and whether the post contained strong or weak co-creation cues — language inviting audiences to participate rather than simply informing them. Posts with high co-creation cues significantly raised perceived source credibility, engagement, and intent to share (e-WOM), and largely wiped out the independent effect of who the sender was. NGO-attributed posts outperformed corporate ones on e-WOM, but only when the post also invited participation; engagement partially mediated the path from credibility to sharing.
studies.why_it_matters: Brands spend heavily on NGO partnerships to borrow credibility for social-impact messaging, but this suggests the format of the message — participatory versus broadcast — does more work than the logo attached to it.
studies.story_angle_primary: A cheap test for communications teams: run matched CSR posts, one informational and one explicitly inviting audience contribution, and compare shares and comments. The experiment suggests participatory framing may be the bigger lever — and that NGO co-branding only pays off on sharing when the post actually asks people to take part, not when it just carries a partner logo.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Skepticism toward corporate do-gooding is widespread, yet this study shows what makes people believe and pass along a social-good message is less about who signed it than whether it treats them as a participant rather than an audience — a useful tell when deciding whether a cause post deserves your share.
studies.caveats: Single country (India, which has a mandated-CSR regime) and a single platform (Facebook); online experiment with stated engagement and sharing intentions rather than observed behavior; stimuli were constructed posts, not live campaigns.
studies.verdict_notes: Design (2x2 between-subjects, 406 active Facebook users in India), the co-creation main effects, the conditional NGO advantage on e-WOM and the partial mediation are all reported correctly; one phrase strengthens "diminishing" into near-elimination.

studies.title: Who really built the new golf league's brand? Content creators the league doesn't control
studies.paper_title: Blending Fairways and Feeds: Co-Creating Brand Meaning in the TMRW Golf League
studies.the_study: Using netnography of league and stakeholder social media content across the creation and first season of the TMRW Golf League — the indoor, tech-driven, extended-reality golf competition — the researchers combined structural topic modeling with qualitative content analysis to trace how brand meaning was negotiated. They find that external new media content creators, not the league's own communications, did much of the work of legitimating and framing the league's novelty, appeal and competitive credibility.
studies.why_it_matters: For any brand launching something genuinely new, the narrative that sticks is substantially authored by third-party creators, which makes creator relations a core part of launch strategy rather than an add-on to paid media.
studies.story_angle_primary: Treat independent creators as co-authors of the launch narrative: map which themes they amplify versus which ones your own channels push, and watch for gaps. The lesson from this case is that legitimacy for an unfamiliar product category tends to be conferred by outsiders — worth building into launch measurement rather than assuming owned media sets the frame.
studies.story_angle_secondary: When a new sport, format or product suddenly feels credible, it is often because a cluster of creators decided it was worth talking about — a reminder of how much of what we accept as 'a real thing' is manufactured in feeds rather than press releases.
studies.caveats: Single-case study of one new league over one season; observational social media content analysis with no causal test; findings are interpretive and may not generalize to other categories or markets.
studies.verdict_notes: Design, methods and core finding match the abstract; the digest sharpens a co-creation finding into a league-vs-creators contrast and generalizes a single netnographic case to "any brand".

studies.title: A century of NFL marketing, read through Black-owned magazines
studies.paper_title: Racelighting through branded entertainment: the historical case of the National Football League
studies.journal: Journal of Historical Research in Marketing
studies.the_study: This viewpoint article assembles 72 media meta-texts — 20 articles from the Crisis (1910–1960), 25 from Ebony (1945–2026), 21 from Jet (1950–2015) and six transcripts of NFL-branded audio/visual content (2014–2026) — and analyzes them thematically and semiotically across four eras of American racial politics. The authors argue the league repeatedly deployed what they term "racelighting": branded entertainment that reads as neutral or progressive on the surface while repurposing Black cultural and political capital to serve commercial and hegemonic interests.
studies.why_it_matters: It puts a century of archival evidence behind a question every brand leader now faces — whether social-justice-adjacent marketing advances a cause or absorbs and defuses it — and shows how the pattern can persist across very different political eras.
studies.story_angle_primary: A reputational stress test for purpose marketing: compare what your campaign claims with how the communities it invokes actually describe it in their own media. The historical pattern here suggests campaigns that align activist imagery with commercial interests tend to be recognized as such by the constituencies involved, long before the mainstream press catches on.
studies.story_angle_secondary: The piece offers a lens for reading sports and brand activism generally — asking who gains cultural power from a gesture of solidarity, and whether a campaign's progressive framing survives contact with the archive of how the same institution behaved in earlier decades.
studies.caveats: Labeled a viewpoint article: interpretive historical and semiotic analysis of a curated archive, not hypothesis testing; single league in a single country; explicitly argued from a critical theoretical standpoint (Afro-pessimism, Racial Formation Theory), so conclusions are contestable readings rather than measured effects.
studies.verdict_notes: Corpus counts, date ranges, method and theoretical framing all match the abstract; one story-angle claim about timing relative to mainstream press is not in the abstract, and "racelighting" is extended rather than coined by the authors.

studies.title: The "terroir paradox": why famous local food can still be invisible in the nearest big city
studies.paper_title: The terroir paradox: institutional barriers to rural–urban food integration in western Türkiye
studies.the_study: Researchers conducted an interpretivist qualitative case study of the food system linking Ödemiş, a rural production district in western Türkiye, with the urban gastronomy market of nearby İzmir, interviewing 17 purposively selected stakeholders (producers, cooperatives, traders and institutional actors) and triangulating with official agricultural statistics and geographical-indication documents. Despite protected-origin potatoes and olive oil and a strong dairy sector, Ödemiş products are barely represented in İzmir restaurants and retail. The barriers were not product quality but rising input costs, logistics gaps, distrust of cooperatives, weak promotion, reliance on informal personal networks instead of institutional channels, and the erosion of knowledge between generations. The authors call this the "terroir paradox": strong production terroir, weak distribution and representation terroir.
studies.why_it_matters: Origin certification and product reputation are often treated as the finish line for regional food branding, but this case suggests the real bottleneck sits in distribution, collective institutions and storytelling — the parts no certificate covers.
studies.story_angle_primary: For brand and category managers working with regional or origin-certified suppliers, this is a prompt to audit the gap between a product's reputational assets and its actual shelf and menu presence — and to ask whether certification budgets would do more work if redirected to logistics, cooperative capacity or trade-facing promotion. One district's experience is a hypothesis to test against your own supply base, not a general law.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For shoppers and diners, it explains why the celebrated specialty from the region an hour away is so hard to find in your own city: the bottleneck is usually trucks, middlemen and broken local institutions, not farming.
studies.caveats: Qualitative case study of a single district–city pair in one country; 17 interviews; no quantitative market or sales data; findings are propositions for comparative testing rather than generalizable estimates.
studies.verdict_notes: Sample, methods and the terroir-paradox framing are faithfully reported; small intensifications ("barely represented", "distrust of cooperatives") and the omission of the study's rural/supply-side vantage point, plus a "usually" generalization in the consumer angle.

studies.title: Students say they care about sustainable eating — but convenience and company decide where they eat
studies.paper_title: Shaping food choices: the influence of nutritional literacy, motivation and eco-concern on young adults' decisions in university canteens
studies.the_study: Researchers surveyed 610 students at the Universities of Bologna and Parma in northern Italy (a convenience sample) and used PLS-SEM to model what drives perceived value of university canteens, combining the motivation–opportunity–ability framework with an eating-related eco-concern questionnaire and a sustainable healthy diet index. Contextual "opportunity" factors — accessibility, convenience and the chance to socialize — were the dominant drivers of perceived value. Individual pro-environmental motivation and personal dietary orientation contributed comparatively little.
studies.why_it_matters: It is a concrete illustration of the gap between green values and everyday food choices: in an institutional setting, the environment people eat in outweighs the attitudes they bring to it.
studies.story_angle_primary: For anyone marketing sustainable food — campus caterers, workplace canteens, grocery retailers — the implication worth testing is that values-based messaging may underperform structural changes to access, speed, price and sociability. Consider running communication and layout/convenience interventions as competing arms rather than assuming persuasion does the heavy lifting.
studies.story_angle_secondary: A useful mirror for consumers: your eco-concern may be real, yet it is probably not what determines today's lunch. Where you eat is largely decided by what is close, quick and shared with friends.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional survey, so no causal claims; convenience sample of students in a single Italian region; measures perceived value and self-reported orientation rather than observed food purchases or waste.
studies.verdict_notes: Sample, journal and modeling details are exact and the body states the outcome correctly, but the headline, "Why it matters" and consumer angle recast a perceived-value outcome as actual choice of where students eat — contradicting the digest's own caveat.

trends_raw:
**Convergent findings**
- **Brand meaning is authored by outsiders.** "Who really built the new golf league's brand? Content creators the league doesn't control" (W7225053690) lands on the same conclusion as last month's "Residents are branding your city whether you invite them to or not" (W7202171291): the entities paying for the brand are not the ones setting its meaning. One is a city, one is a new sports property, and both find that unplanned, third-party meaning-making outweighs owned channels.
- **Information-deficit thinking keeps failing.** "Consumers say they'd rather be regulated than lectured on plastic" (W7225111854) and "Students say they care about sustainable eating — but convenience and company decide where they eat" (W7223028679) both locate the binding constraint outside the individual's head, echoing "Why free pads don't get used" (W7214428578) and "Not all opposition is persuadable" (W7214777517). The prior digest found the non-informational barrier to be social (stigma, moral orientation); this batch finds it material (no refill point, no proximity, no time).
- **CSR communication audited against what the organization actually does.** "A century of NFL marketing, read through Black-owned magazines" (W7225126842) extends the argument of "India's bidi industry borrowed Big Tobacco's playbook" (W7220403023) — social-impact communication as reputational cover — from supply-chain evidence to a century of archival evidence.

**Advances**
- **AI in PR moves from role identity to market compulsion and governance vacuum.** The previous digest established that AI is reshaping PR roles toward judgment and ethical stewardship ("The PR manager's job is quietly becoming 'ethical advisor to the machine,'" W7213310447) and that organizational support, not individual training, predicted effectiveness ("AI training didn't move the needle," W7205004055). The new batch explains *why* adoption is happening anyway: "PR practitioners say using AI is no longer a choice" (W7222613543) documents competitive anxiety rather than measured results as the driver, with governance left to individual discretion — the precise gap W7205004055 implied mattered. "PR agencies are quietly using AI — but in Arabic, humans are still doing the hard part" (W7221812755) adds a cost dimension the earlier work missed: the efficiency case thins sharply outside English.
- **Crisis communication capability as organizational infrastructure.** "What makes communicators feel like crisis leaders: ethics support and equity resources" (W7211909650) advances "Why crisis playbooks break down in practice" (W7203759226). The earlier study found practitioners knew the right response and were overruled; this one identifies what institutional backing appears to strengthen their standing under pressure.
- **Sustainability claims versus the system behind them.** "Why companies cannot count the emissions hiding in their supply base" (W7224156801) and "When populism rises, green packaging quietly disappears" (W7214508893) push the previous digest's CSR-credibility thread (W7220403023) from labor exposure into measurement and political contingency.

**Counterpoints**
- **Does formal apparatus do anything?** The previous digest's running theme was that paperwork underperforms visible behavior ("Compliance programs barely work on their own," W7213244866; "AI training didn't move the needle," W7205004055). "What makes communicators feel like crisis leaders" (W7211909650) complicates that: here, perceived *access* to ethics resources and equity support mediated the relationship between work strain and crisis leadership. The outcome is a self-reported perception rather than observed behavior, so the two sit in tension rather than contradiction — worth watching whether formal resources matter more for practitioner capability than for employee conduct.
- **Does green positioning pay?** "Green business models scale just as well as the ordinary kind" (W7224854055) deflates both the cost and the growth-engine stories about environmental ambition, where the previous digest's "symbolic promotions" work (W7215933723) suggested values-based appeals could carry real commercial lift. The distinction appears to be identity-based appeals (which moved sales) versus environmental ambition as a business-model attribute (which did not move scaling either way).

**New themes**
- **Audience response to corporate AI talk**, not just internal AI practice: "Talking up AI wins positive sentiment but loses audience" (W7208830817) is the first study across either digest to measure how publics react to AI messaging.
- **Message format over source identity** in CSR: "In CSR posts, inviting people in beats who's doing the talking" (W7223321733) challenges the NGO-partnership credibility-borrowing model, which neither digest had tested before.
- **Epistemic credibility as an engagement driver**: "Big Pharma's pandemic tweets: dry facts beat upbeat framing" (W7223996694).
- **Distribution as the missing half of origin branding**: "The 'terroir paradox'" (W7223808860) introduces place-of-origin reputation economics, absent from the previous run.
feature_pitch_raw:
**The pattern:** Five studies in this batch, approaching from completely different directions, find that green commitments are governed by politics, logistics and infrastructure rather than by consumer conviction or corporate intent. Firms cut back on eco-friendly packaging when the political signal turned ("When populism rises, green packaging quietly disappears," W7214508893); most of a firm's footprint sits in a supply base it structurally cannot count, with sourcing diversification inflating it ("Why companies cannot count the emissions hiding in their supply base," W7224156801); consumers name missing refill and return systems rather than ignorance as the barrier and rank regulation above information campaigns ("Consumers say they'd rather be regulated than lectured on plastic," W7225111854); canteen users' choices are driven by access, speed and sociability rather than eco-concern ("Students say they care about sustainable eating," W7223028679); and strong environmental ambition neither helped nor hindered scaling, which turned on revenue diversification ("Green business models scale just as well as the ordinary kind," W7224854055).

**Why pitch this now:** Scope 3 disclosure is moving from voluntary to mandatory across several reporting regimes just as "greenhushing" spreads and political hostility to climate policy intensifies — so brands are being required to publish numbers they cannot verify about a footprint they do not control, while the consumer-education campaigns that filled the gap turn out to be aimed at the wrong constraint.

**Angle:** A feature on sustainability marketing as a structural problem misdiagnosed as a persuasion problem — written for brand, packaging and corporate affairs leaders deciding what to promise next, with a strong secondary read for consumers who have been told their choices are the lever.

**Potential headlines:**
- Green Packaging Tracks Politics More Closely Than It Tracks Shoppers
- Consumers Keep Asking to Be Regulated. Brands Keep Sending Them Leaflets.
- The Climate Promise on Your Packaging Rests on Numbers Nobody Can Check

**Potential outlets:**
- **Marketing Week** — its readership is actively defending sustainability positioning to finance directors, and the finding that green ambition is commercially neutral rather than a growth driver directly reframes that argument.
- **Retail Dive** — the refill-and-return infrastructure gap and private-label packaging retreat are retail operations stories, not just messaging ones.
- **Bloomberg Green** — the Scope 3 measurement study and the Paris-exit packaging retreat fit its corporate climate-accountability reporting, which already tracks disclosure quality.
- **Grist** — runs consumer-facing work skeptical of individual-responsibility framing, and the plastics and canteen studies hand it empirical backing for that case.

- **When populism rises, green packaging quietly disappears (Work ID W7214508893):** A difference-in-differences study showing CPG firms quietly dialed back eco-packaging after the Paris exit announcement — sustainability as a political variable, not a brand value — for a CMO-audience column or a business-section piece on greenhushing.
- **Big Pharma's pandemic tweets: dry facts beat upbeat framing (Work ID W7223996694):** 6,466 tweets suggesting that amplifying what is true outperforms rebutting what is false, and neutral framing beats positive framing — for a PR-trade analysis on misinformation response playbooks.
- **Why companies cannot count the emissions hiding in their supply base (Work ID W7224156801):** Supplier diversification, usually sold as resilience, appears to inflate the emissions a brand will have to report and defend — for a supply-chain or sustainability-trade explainer, or a corporate-finance piece on disclosure risk.
- **Consumers say they'd rather be regulated than lectured on plastic (Work ID W7225111854):** Shoppers ranked incentives and rules above information campaigns, suggesting that publicly backing regulation may be less reputationally risky than brands assume — for a public-affairs or packaging-trade piece, or a consumer column on the misplaced burden of individual virtue.
- **Green business models scale just as well as the ordinary kind (Work ID W7224854055):** Across 21 sharing-mobility providers, revenue diversification separated winners from losers while environmental ambition did neither — for a mobility or startup-strategy trade piece puncturing both sides of the green-growth argument.
- **PR agencies are quietly using AI — but in Arabic, humans are still doing the hard part (Work ID W7221812755):** The efficiency case for AI in communications collapses outside English, with cultural correction done as invisible, unbudgeted human labor — for an agency-trade feature or a general-interest piece on the hidden labor behind AI output.
- **What makes communicators feel like crisis leaders: ethics support and equity resources (Work ID W7211909650):** A survey of 1,044 practitioners pointing to ethics counsel and equity support as crisis-readiness infrastructure rather than HR extras — for a PR-trade management column.
- **Talking up AI wins positive sentiment but loses audience (Work ID W7208830817):** Corporate AI posts drew positive sentiment but less engagement, with the penalty erased by CSR framing and absent at tech firms where AI is simply expected — for a marketing-trade news analysis on how to announce AI without boring your audience.
- **PR practitioners say using AI is no longer a choice (Work ID W7222613543):** Adoption driven by competitive fear rather than evidence of better outcomes, with governance resting on individual discretion in the absence of rules — for a PR-trade feature or a work-and-technology piece in a general-interest outlet.
- **In CSR posts, inviting people in beats who's doing the talking (Work ID W7223321733):** An experiment suggesting participatory framing does more for credibility and sharing than an NGO partner's logo — a cheap A/B test for comms teams, for a social-impact marketing trade brief.
- **Who really built the new golf league's brand? (Work ID W7225053690):** Independent creators, not the league, conferred legitimacy on an unfamiliar format — making creator relations a launch-strategy function, for a sports-marketing or creator-economy trade feature.
- **A century of NFL marketing, read through Black-owned magazines (Work ID W7225126842):** A hundred years of archival evidence that branded solidarity gets recognized as commercial appropriation by the communities invoked long before the mainstream press notices — for a culture or sports-business feature, or a purpose-marketing essay.
- **The "terroir paradox" (Work ID W7223808860):** Protected-origin products that are invisible in the city an hour away, because the bottleneck is trucks, middlemen and broken cooperatives rather than quality or certification — for a food-trade explainer or a general-interest food feature on why local specialties don't travel.
- **Students say they care about sustainable eating — but convenience and company decide where they eat (Work ID W7223028679):** Access, speed and sociability outweighed eco-concern in 610 students' canteen choices — for a foodservice-trade piece or a consumer-psychology explainer on the value-action gap.

# Fact-Check Report: Marketing Research Digest — Public Relations & Reputation — 2026-11-03
**Checked:** 2026-11-03 | **Studies reviewed:** 14
**Primary audience:** marketers and brand leaders | **Secondary audience:** general readers and consumers

---

### Study 1: When populism rises, green packaging quietly disappears
**Work ID:** W7214508893 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract.

### Study 2: Big Pharma's pandemic tweets: dry facts beat upbeat framing
**Work ID:** W7223996694 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract.

### Study 3: Why companies cannot count the emissions hiding in their supply base
**Work ID:** W7224156801 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Share of footprint overstated** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Most of a consumer brand's carbon footprint sits with its suppliers"
- **Abstract says:** "However, a substantial portion of emissions occurs beyond these boundaries, and firms continue to struggle to identify, measure, and manage emissions embedded in their supply bases."
- **Problem:** The abstract says a "substantial portion" of emissions lies beyond Scope 1 and 2; the digest asserts a majority, and repeats it as "the far bigger share" in the consumer angle. The abstract does not quantify the share.
- **Suggested fix:** "Change to "A substantial portion of a consumer brand's carbon footprint sits with its suppliers" and soften "far bigger share" to "the portion buried in its suppliers.""

### Study 4: Consumers say they'd rather be regulated than lectured on plastic
**Work ID:** W7225111854 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract.

### Study 5: Green business models scale just as well as the ordinary kind — but only via the same boring levers
**Work ID:** W7224854055 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Failure configurations over-specified** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "half-committing (green claims without matching public-sector alignment) sits in the failure configurations"
- **Abstract says:** "Third, successfully scaled business models exhibit congruence between environmental ambitions and public alignment."
- **Problem:** The abstract reports congruence among successfully scaled models; it does not describe the content of the two failure configurations, so attributing "green claims without matching public-sector alignment" to them is an inference presented as a finding.
- **Suggested fix:** "Reword to "successfully scaled firms showed congruence between green ambitions and public alignment, so half-committing may not pay off" without naming the failure configurations."

### Study 6: PR agencies are quietly using AI — but in Arabic, humans are still doing the hard part
**Work ID:** W7221812755 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Generalization beyond Arabic** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "this suggests the efficiency case for AI in communications weakens sharply outside English"
- **Abstract says:** "Adoption is early-stage and selective ... inhibited by skills gaps, limited Arabic-language tooling and unclear governance ... ethical risks are compounded in Arab settings by cultural–linguistic fit and uneven institutional support."
- **Problem:** The evidence concerns Arabic-language tooling in the Arab region; "outside English" and "weakens sharply" extend the claim to all non-English languages with a magnitude the abstract never states.
- **Suggested fix:** "Rephrase as "the efficiency case appears weaker where language tooling is thin, as the authors report for Arabic.""

### Study 7: What makes communicators feel like crisis leaders: ethics support and equity resources
**Work ID:** W7211909650 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Perceptions reported as performance** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "as levers that may strengthen how communications teams perform and see themselves under pressure"
- **Abstract says:** "Results suggest that all three factors ... generate significant effects on crisis leadership perceptions."
- **Problem:** Every measure in this cross-sectional survey is a practitioner perception, including the outcome; no performance was assessed. The body text sits awkwardly against the digest's own caveat.
- **Suggested fix:** "Drop "perform and" so the sentence refers only to how teams see themselves and their work under pressure."

### Study 8: Talking up AI wins positive sentiment but loses audience — unless you tie it to social good
**Work ID:** W7208830817 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Effect size overstated** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "framing AI within a corporate social responsibility context erased much of that engagement penalty"
- **Abstract says:** "Yet framing AI within the context of CSR mitigates this engagement penalty."
- **Problem:** "Mitigates" indicates reduction of unspecified magnitude; "erased much of" implies a quantified, near-complete offset the abstract does not report.
- **Suggested fix:** "Use "reduced that engagement penalty.""

### Study 9: PR practitioners say using AI is no longer a choice — it is the price of staying competitive
**Work ID:** W7222613543 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract.

### Study 10: In CSR posts, inviting people in beats who's doing the talking
**Work ID:** W7223321733 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Source effect overstated** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "largely wiped out the independent effect of who the sender was"
- **Abstract says:** "High co-creation cues significantly increased source credibility, consumer engagement, and e-WOM, diminishing the independent effect of message source."
- **Problem:** The abstract says the independent source effect was diminished, not eliminated; "largely wiped out" implies a stronger result than reported.
- **Suggested fix:** "Use "diminished the independent effect of who the sender was.""

### Study 11: Who really built the new golf league's brand? Content creators the league doesn't control
**Work ID:** W7225053690 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Creators framed as displacing the league's own communications** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "They find that external new media content creators, not the league's own communications, did much of the work of legitimating and framing the league's novelty, appeal and competitive credibility."
- **Abstract says:** "The study's findings highlight the role played by external actors in legitimating and framing the league's novelty, appeal, and competition."
- **Problem:** The abstract reports a co-creation finding — external actors played a (discrete) role alongside the league and other stakeholders. It does not say external creators did more of this work than the league's own channels, and no comparative weighting is reported.
- **Suggested fix:** "Rewrite as: "External new media content creators played a distinct role in legitimating and framing the league's novelty, appeal and competition, alongside the league's own communications.""

**Issue B. Single case generalized in "Why it matters"** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "For any brand launching something genuinely new, the narrative that sticks is substantially authored by third-party creators, which makes creator relations a core part of launch strategy rather than an add-on to paid media."
- **Abstract says:** "Through a netnographic analysis of league and stakeholder social media content during the league's creation and staging of its first season ... the study investigates actor performativity in brand co-creation."
- **Problem:** An interpretive single-case netnography of one new golf league cannot support a claim about "any brand launching something genuinely new"; the caveats acknowledge this but the framing does not.
- **Suggested fix:** "Hedge to: "In this case, much of the legitimating narrative came from third-party creators — a prompt to consider creator relations in launches of unfamiliar categories.""

### Study 12: A century of NFL marketing, read through Black-owned magazines
**Work ID:** W7225126842 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Unsupported claim about mainstream press lag** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "The historical pattern here suggests campaigns that align activist imagery with commercial interests tend to be recognized as such by the constituencies involved, long before the mainstream press catches on."
- **Abstract says:** "The findings elucidate the branding strategy of NFL entertainment as documented in black-oriented periodicals, which saw black resistance repurposed for white ends by leveraging the political and epistemological meanings of racial struggle to maintain control over historically dynamic processes."
- **Problem:** The abstract documents how Black-oriented periodicals depicted the NFL's strategy, but makes no comparison with mainstream press coverage or its timing; the digest invents a comparative claim.
- **Suggested fix:** "Drop "long before the mainstream press catches on" or rephrase to note that Black-oriented periodicals documented these dynamics at the time."

**Issue B. Term attribution** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "The authors argue the league repeatedly deployed what they term "racelighting""
- **Abstract says:** "the authors extend "racelighting" (RL) as a conceptual framework"
- **Problem:** The abstract says the authors extend an existing concept rather than coin it, so "what they term" slightly misattributes the term.
- **Suggested fix:** "Change to "what the authors, extending an existing concept, call 'racelighting'"."

### Study 13: The "terroir paradox": why famous local food can still be invisible in the nearest big city
**Work ID:** W7223808860 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Intensified wording on market presence and cooperatives** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Ödemiş products are barely represented in İzmir restaurants and retail. The barriers were not product quality but rising input costs, logistics gaps, distrust of cooperatives"
- **Abstract says:** "Despite strong gastronomic capacity, including GI-registered potatoes and olive oil and a strong dairy sector, Ödemiş remains underrepresented in İzmir. Key barriers include rising input costs, logistics deficits and negative assessments of cooperative effectiveness."
- **Problem:** "Barely represented" is stronger than "underrepresented", "restaurants and retail" is more specific than "İzmir's urban gastronomy market", and "distrust of cooperatives" recasts negative assessments of cooperative effectiveness as distrust.
- **Suggested fix:** "Use the abstract's wording: "underrepresented in İzmir's urban gastronomy market" and "negative views of how effective cooperatives are"."

**Issue B. Perspective of informants not noted** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "interviewing 17 purposively selected stakeholders (producers, cooperatives, traders and institutional actors)"
- **Abstract says:** "This study examines how Ödemiş's rural food production connects with İzmir's urban gastronomy market in western Türkiye, primarily from the perspective of rural and locally embedded food-system actors."
- **Problem:** The abstract does not break the 17 informants into those four categories and explicitly states the vantage point is primarily rural/locally embedded actors — meaning urban buyers' views are largely absent, a relevant limitation when barriers are reported as fact.
- **Suggested fix:** "Say "17 purposively selected stakeholders, primarily rural and locally embedded food-system actors" and note in caveats that urban-market actors' perspectives are largely absent."

**Issue C. Single case generalized in consumer angle** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "it explains why the celebrated specialty from the region an hour away is so hard to find in your own city: the bottleneck is usually trucks, middlemen and broken local institutions, not farming"
- **Abstract says:** "The framework extends production-centric understandings of terroir and offers propositions for comparative testing."
- **Problem:** The authors present propositions for comparative testing from one district–city pair; "usually" implies an established general pattern.
- **Suggested fix:** "Replace "usually" with "in this case" or "can be"."

### Study 14: Students say they care about sustainable eating — but convenience and company decide where they eat
**Work ID:** W7223028679 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Perceived value presented as eating behavior** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "Students say they care about sustainable eating — but convenience and company decide where they eat"
- **Abstract says:** "Results indicate that contextual opportunities – such as accessibility and socialization – are the primary drivers of students' perceived values of university canteens, while individual pro-environmental motivation and dietary orientation play a limited role"
- **Problem:** The modeled outcome is perceived value of canteen services, not where students choose to eat; the headline and the consumer angle ("Where you eat is largely decided by what is close, quick and shared with friends") assert a behavioral outcome the study did not measure, contradicting the digest's own caveat.
- **Suggested fix:** "Reframe as "what students value in a university canteen is driven more by access and sociability than by eco-concern" and adjust the consumer angle accordingly."

**Issue B. Nature of the attitude–behavior gap** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "It is a concrete illustration of the gap between green values and everyday food choices"
- **Abstract says:** "suggesting a potential gap between pro-environmental intentions and actual perception of the institutional food environment"
- **Problem:** The abstract describes a potential gap between intentions and how students perceive the food environment, not between values and observed food choices.
- **Suggested fix:** "Change to "a potential gap between pro-environmental intentions and how students perceive the institutional food environment"."

**Issue C. Added driver not in abstract** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Contextual "opportunity" factors — accessibility, convenience and the chance to socialize — were the dominant drivers of perceived value."
- **Abstract says:** "contextual opportunities – such as accessibility and socialization – are the primary drivers"
- **Problem:** "Convenience" is added to the list of named contextual factors; the abstract names only accessibility and socialization.
- **Suggested fix:** "List only accessibility and socialization, or mark convenience as the digest's own gloss."

## Issue Summary

| Study # | Headline | Verdict | Notes |
|---------|----------|---------|-------|
| 1 | When populism rises, green packaging quietly disappears | ✅ Accurate | Design (quasi-natural experiment, difference-in-differences, global CPG launch sample), direction of effect, and both moderators (economic freedom, cultural tightness) are reported faithfully; caveats correctly note the observational design and absence of consumer outcomes. |
| 2 | Big Pharma's pandemic tweets: dry facts beat upbeat framing | ✅ Accurate | Sample (6,466 tweets, six firms, 2020-2021), methods, and all three findings match the abstract; correlational nature and single-platform/single-industry limits are flagged. |
| 3 | Why companies cannot count the emissions hiding in their supply base | ⚠️ Minor issues | Sample (1,142 firms), drivers and moderators are reported correctly; the "Why it matters" and consumer angle upgrade the abstract's "substantial portion" of emissions to "most"/"far bigger share." |
| 4 | Consumers say they'd rather be regulated than lectured on plastic | ✅ Accurate | Mixed-method design (20 interviews plus best-worst scaling survey of 400), New Zealand milk packaging context, barrier findings and policy preferences all match; the digest correctly frames these as stated preferences. The citizen-role list omits "collective support," a trivial truncation. |
| 5 | Green business models scale just as well as the ordinary kind — but only via the same boring levers | ⚠️ Minor issues | fsQCA on 21 providers, five design choices, six configurations (four success, two failure) and the three implications are accurately conveyed; one marketer angle states a claim about the failure configurations that the abstract does not make. |
| 6 | PR agencies are quietly using AI — but in Arabic, humans are still doing the hard part | ⚠️ Minor issues | Method (20 interviews across six countries plus directed content analysis), adoption areas, drivers, barriers and the sociolinguistic-labour argument all match; the "Why it matters" generalizes beyond Arabic to all non-English contexts. |
| 7 | What makes communicators feel like crisis leaders: ethics support and equity resources | ⚠️ Minor issues | N=1,044, the 42.7% experience figure, and the mediation structure (ethics resources and equity support mediating work challenge; crisis communication effectiveness intervening in the indirect effects) are all reported correctly; the "Why it matters" slips from perceptions to performance. |
| 8 | Talking up AI wins positive sentiment but loses audience — unless you tie it to social good | ⚠️ Minor issues | Mixed-method Korean design, instrumental framing finding, engagement penalty, CSR moderation and the conventional-vs-high-tech contrast are all present; one verb overstates the size of the CSR effect. |
| 9 | PR practitioners say using AI is no longer a choice — it is the price of staying competitive | ✅ Accurate | N=22 interviews, the compulsory/self-optimization/productivity narratives, the role of field dispositions and the absence of regulatory frameworks all match the abstract; caveats appropriately note the theory-driven reading and lack of outcome data. Singular "the author" is unverifiable from the abstract alone but harmless. |
| 10 | In CSR posts, inviting people in beats who's doing the talking | ⚠️ Minor issues | Design (2x2 between-subjects, 406 active Facebook users in India), the co-creation main effects, the conditional NGO advantage on e-WOM and the partial mediation are all reported correctly; one phrase strengthens "diminishing" into near-elimination. |
| 11 | Who really built the new golf league's brand? Content creators the league doesn't control | ⚠️ Minor issues | Design, methods and core finding match the abstract; the digest sharpens a co-creation finding into a league-vs-creators contrast and generalizes a single netnographic case to "any brand". |
| 12 | A century of NFL marketing, read through Black-owned magazines | ⚠️ Minor issues | Corpus counts, date ranges, method and theoretical framing all match the abstract; one story-angle claim about timing relative to mainstream press is not in the abstract, and "racelighting" is extended rather than coined by the authors. |
| 13 | The "terroir paradox": why famous local food can still be invisible in the nearest big city | ⚠️ Minor issues | Sample, methods and the terroir-paradox framing are faithfully reported; small intensifications ("barely represented", "distrust of cooperatives") and the omission of the study's rural/supply-side vantage point, plus a "usually" generalization in the consumer angle. |
| 14 | Students say they care about sustainable eating — but convenience and company decide where they eat | ⚠️ Minor issues | Sample, journal and modeling details are exact and the body states the outcome correctly, but the headline, "Why it matters" and consumer angle recast a perceived-value outcome as actual choice of where students eat — contradicting the digest's own caveat. |

**Total issues:** 16 (12 Minor, 4 Moderate, 0 Major)
**Entries requiring revision:** 10
